title: Price rises just before the 2025 promotions

brief.decision: Which 2025 promotions to review first with the legal team, and whether to freeze list prices in the two weeks before every promotion from next year, since a discount taken off a list price raised just before it makes the advertised saving look bigger than it is

expected_output.grain: one row per promotion that started in 2025

checkpoints.prompt: Joost wants to know, for each product of a promotion that started in 2025, whether the discount was taken off a list price Voltmarkt had raised just before the promotion began. Which comparison answers that?

options.text: The product's latest list price in price_history against its first list price, which shows how far the product's price moved over its whole life on sale
The average unit price customers paid on the promotion's order lines against the product's list price, which shows how much discount they really got
The list price of the version in effect on the start_date against the product's previous version, and how many days before the start the newer one began
The list price on 31 December 2025 against the list price on the start_date, since a price that rose after the promotion shows that the discount was not real

checkpoints.prompt: Joost's check covers every product of every promotion that started in 2025. Take the promotions with a start_date from 1 January to 31 December 2025, both days included, and count their rows in promotion_products, so a product that is in two such promotions counts twice. How many promoted products is that? Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Joost's question.

Joost's headline is the share of promoted products whose list price was raised just before their promotion. Take every product of every promotion with a start_date from 1 January to 31 December 2025, both days included, once for each such promotion it is in (its rows in promotion_products). For each, use the product's price version in effect on the promotion's start_date: valid_from on or before that day, and valid_to on or after it or missing. The product counts as raised when that version's list_price_eur is higher than the list_price_eur of the same product's version just before it (within a product, versions follow each other by valid_from) and that version took effect 0 to 14 days before the start_date (start_date minus valid_from is from 0 to 14). A version with no version before it is not raised. What percentage of the promoted products were raised? Type the percentage rounded to 1 decimal, for example 12.3.

Joost's table for the 2025 promotions shows that a few percent of the promoted products had their list price raised in the 14 days before their promotion began, that about as many had their list price cut in those same days, and that the largest rises were in Black Week. A colleague says this proves Voltmarkt raised list prices on purpose to make its discounts look bigger. What should Joost answer?

options.text: The colleague is right: any rise in the two weeks before a promotion makes its discount fake, so every promotion with a raised product misled customers and should go to legal.
Probably not: the rises are small next to the promotions' discounts, so customers still got a real discount, and there is nothing in the table for legal to review.
The colleague is right: Black Week had the largest rises, well above any other promotion's, and that shows every 2025 promotion's list prices were planned in the same way.
Not from this table alone: cuts were about as common as rises in those days, which looks like routine repricing; first ask who made the large Black Week rises and why.

checkpoints.prompt: Write 2 to 4 sentences for Joost that you could say aloud in 60 seconds: the headline number, whether the rises look planned, one caveat and one next step before Thursday's meeting with legal.

model_plan:
Metric formula: for each product of each promotion that started in 2025, the list price of the version in effect on the start_date against the price of the same product's version before it (LAG over valid_from, partitioned by product); raised when the price went up and that version took effect 0 to 14 days before the start_date, cut when it went down in the same days; per promotion, the number of products, the raised and cut counts, and the largest rise as a percentage of the old price, rounded to 1 decimal.
Output grain: one row per promotion that started in 2025.
Tables and keys: price_history for the versions (product_id, valid_from); promotions joined to promotion_products on promo_id, and each product joined to its version in effect on the start_date.
Filters: promotions with a start_date from 1 January to 31 December 2025; the version with valid_from on or before the start_date and valid_to on or after it or missing.
Edge cases: a product's first version has no version before it, so it is neither raised nor cut; the previous price must come from the same product, so the window needs a partition by product; joining every earlier version instead of the one in effect counts a product many times; a promotion with no raised product has a missing largest rise.
Expected row count: 30
model_answer_template: {CP4} percent of the {CP2} promoted products in Voltmarkt's 2025 promotions had their list price raised in the two weeks before the promotion began, and about as many had a cut in those weeks, so most rises look like routine repricing rather than a plan to inflate discounts. The exception is Black Week, where the largest rises sit, well above any other promotion's, so those products should go to legal first. The check compares each price only with the version just before it and cannot say why a price changed, so a rise made earlier or in two steps can slip through. Before Thursday, I would find out who changed the Black Week prices and propose a freeze on list prices for promoted products in the two weeks before every promotion.
follow_up_question: Which Black Week products had their list price raised, and who approved those changes?
